speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As Members on both sides of this House are aware, the state of inflation in Singapore is not good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also close to double the average since our nation's Independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The pain of this rising cost of living is even more keenly felt by the average household and small business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Food inflation is up to 4.5%, more than three times higher than last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While news headlines and my mother's constant reminders focus on costly chicken and the threat to what most would consider our national dish, chicken rice, prices of all kinds of meat are up almost 6%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Eggs are about 30% pricier and even those choosing a healthier diet face vegetables that are 5% more expensive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another area where prices have shot up is energy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am certain I am not the only Member here who has received irate emails from residents who have expressed shock and dismay at their utilities bills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Electricity is up 20% – dearer than it was a year ago – and gas, more than 10%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This not only means that more of us have to think twice before turning the air conditioner on; it also means that our small businesses, already operating on lower sales because of the pandemic, face even thinner margins.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With fuel prices up by a quarter, it is unsurprising that transportation is now more expensive, with price rises in the teens, compared to a year ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not affecting just those who have the luxury of owning cars or getting on planes for the holidays.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Public transportation costs are up more than 7%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For families that rely on the occasional taxi or private hire car (PHC) to get their kids to school when they are running late, this option has become that much more difficult.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When the prices of what we eat, getting to work and keeping our homes and businesses running are all rising rapidly, this is not an inflation problem any longer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is, therefore, incumbent on policymakers to do what they can to alleviate the pain felt by the people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, the drivers of inflation are multifaceted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A significant part of inflation is global in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, the prices of commodities, such as food and energy, have climbed higher since the middle of last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The war in Ukraine fed further uncertainty and led to spikes in the prices of wheat, corn and sunflower oil.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Supply chain pressures, not just in China, where the administration's stubborn adherence to a zero-COVID policy has led to rolling lockdowns, but also globally, have meant more upward pressure on prices for the rest of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Tight labour markets worldwide have seen wages add their own powerful contribution to the inflation mix.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At first glance, such imported inflation looks like something beyond our control since we are a small open economy and price taker in global markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is incorrect to insist that inflation must be a storm, that we simply need a lull time to pass.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The experience of advanced economies that are around a half-year ahead of us in confronting the price dragon suggests that inflation may, like the last drunk uninvited guest at a party, hang around longer than we would like or appreciate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Their central banks have already abandoned rhetoric that the phenomenon is transitory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With the source of inflation emanating domestically, it behooves us to act locally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are genuine consequences for failing to act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In addition to the real cost borne by various segments of the population, refraining from decisive action now could allow inflation to become even more entrenched in expectations of our households and businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This runs the risk that inflation becomes more permanent than temporary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The role of macroeconomic policy is to stabilise the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In most economies, the first line of defence against inflation is the central bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But as explained yesterday by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, our nation's central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), does not operate as a traditional central bank relying on short-term interest rates to manage price pressures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Instead, it subordinates the policy rate to exchange rate considerations consistent with our open economy and considerable exposure to international trade and financial flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Regardless of whether one agrees with this approach – I, for one, do – it is also well understood that, having adopted such a target, we can no longer control inflation via traditional interest rate hikes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, thankfully, this does not mean that there are no other tools in MAS' toolkit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One strategy, developed in recent decades, is to intervene in markets for financial assets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some of us may be familiar with the process of quantitative easing, or QE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The central bank makes large-scale asset purchases to keep long-term interest rates low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The objective of QE is to stimulate the economy in the face of interest rates that are close to zero.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over the past decade, QE was applied by major developed economies' central banks, such as the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve, with some success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Quantitative tightening, or QT, is essentially the opposite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Central banks would intervene in markets to sell longer-term government bonds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whether via QT or other means, it strikes me as eminently reasonable that MAS attempts to elevate such long rates so that the real interest rate – that is, the interest rate, net of inflation	– would no longer be negative, as it currently is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would represent a genuine tightening of monetary conditions, which is what is necessary to contain inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the most direct approach to controlling inflation in the context of our current policy framework is to have MAS target a stronger Singapore dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am also keenly sensitive to how MAS operates best when left with relative free rein over how they conduct the more technical elements of monetary and exchange rate policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, as I shared with this House earlier this year, while the execution of policies is, indeed, best left to experts, the choice of what policy we pursue falls appropriately within the domain of politicians, who are best positioned to debate the relative merits or trade-offs that affect the welfare of the people we represent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is with this in mind that I am broaching the issue of our exchange rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that we can do more to strengthen the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will reduce the cost of imported goods and services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since much of what we consume is imported, a strong Singapore dollar can, in turn, lower domestic inflation as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is unclear how much this effort to strengthen the Singapore dollar has succeeded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is because, of the three moves, only the most recent one was sufficiently aggressive, involving an adjustment of not just the slope but also the midpoint of the policy band, while the other two were more limited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are many reasons why this may be the case, not least because the US dollar has been exceptionally strong, even compared to other currencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the reality is that the Singapore dollar is, today, weaker in terms of the currency that global commodities like oil, gas and agricultural products are priced in, which is the US dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This translates into higher prices here as higher import prices pass through into domestic inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The efforts of MAS are demonstrably too tentative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is worse is that we will risk falling behind the curve even further as the Federal Reserve recently moved to hike interest rates more aggressively, which will further fuel appreciation of the US dollar unless we act more aggressively ourselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sure, such a policy will entail winners and losers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We would be concerned about what the effects of a strong exchange rate could mean for exports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there are reasons to believe that currency appreciation need not be that problematic in our modern Singapore economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not forget that our entrepreneurial model and natural resource scarcity mean that our producers often import raw materials and other intermediate inputs to production, which all benefit from a stronger Singapore dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our economy is also less reliant on manufacturing than before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, a number of our tradeable services in finance, information and communications technology (ICT) and professional services have pricing power, which allows them to be more resilient to exchange rate fluctuations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By the same token, capital inflows may also remain unaffected by currency appreciation and could even potentially increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, multinationals based here can manage their foreign exchange rate risk through hedging as long as plans for doing so are telegraphed in advance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the long run, a stronger currency may provide the impetus for our local firms to finally upgrade their operations to reflect higher productivity and quality rather than competing solely on low prices and cost-cutting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are, of course, reasons for caution on this front.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even casual students of international economic history will have encountered the Plaza Accord, an agreement struck between then leading nations to intervene in currency markets to strengthen the Japanese yen and the German Deutsche Mark relative to the US dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The result was a success but some observers have argued that the concerted intervention set in motion the Japanese real estate and stock market bubble and the economy's subsequent Lost Decade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We do not want that here, but even so, there is ample evidence that we can afford more strengthening of the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Standard metrics for comparing the under- and over-valuation of our currency suggest that the Singapore dollar is, indeed, significantly undervalued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is latent demand for the Singapore dollar as an attractive safe haven currency in these tumultuous times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, paradoxically, we may not even need to spend that much to prop up our currency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It may be as simple as ceasing interventions that restrain our exchange rate and allowing foreign exchange markets to work more efficiently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a luxury that precious few countries can afford but one that we can leverage now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These monetary and exchange rate moves should occur alongside fiscal policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would suggest three general principles that guide our thinking on this matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, we should subscribe to the general principle of being timely, targeted and temporary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have already outlined why support is needed now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, it is timely, given how a souring of the global economic environment means that we must rely less on global growth tailwinds to support our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Targeting specific groups and keeping the policy temporary will also minimise the budgetary footprint at a time when we have already drawn liberally from our reserves and the economy is on track towards a self-sustaining recovery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, our fiscal balances should not be building up excess surpluses at this time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that increased revenues resulting from higher collections of various taxes and duties should, as far as possible, be rebated back to citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This ensures that our Government does not enjoy a windfall gain, while our citizens suffer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While tempting, since it automates the process of wage adjustment to rising inflation, the experience of emerging markets in the 1980s and 1990s is a testament that this well-meaning policy can end up institutionalising inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the package announced last month by MOF is based on three somewhat different philosophies, it also embeds some of the principles that I have mentioned of being temporary and targeted and relying on better than expected fiscal outturns from the prior fiscal year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One important example of policy that follows these principles is to make adjustments for Singaporeans on fixed incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An elderly person spending $20 a day may now only be able to buy one prata instead of two for breakfast, may be forced to skip their afternoon tea or order two instead of three items of "cai png".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is worse is that this diminished consumption will be with them for the rest of their lives even when inflation has returned to normal rates, because elevated prices do not automatically come back down even when inflation disappears.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inflation of 3% above the historical average would mean that their retirement funds now buy 3% less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In practical terms, this means adjustments for those that rely on ComCare and CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have to remind ourselves that while financial markets can and do adjust returns to reflect higher inflation, this is not the case for those locked into a fixed income stream.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For retirees, CPF returns have remained unchanged thus far, even as higher prices mean that whatever these retirees have set aside in savings will now buy less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For Comcare, the announced increase for Long-Term Assistance is surely welcome, but it is unclear why a comparable degree of support is not extended for short- and medium-term assistance, since inflation hits both types of households in much the same way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can be funded by the returns paid on Special Singapore Government Securities, or SSGS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The higher returns on SSGS can, in turn, be made up from higher nominal returns that would accrue from financial assets that are marked to market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Macroeconomic policies are often viewed as blunt instruments: they affect the economy on the aggregate; and hence, we may be concerned that pushing these levers may be too disruptive for an economy that is already on a tentative road to recovery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the contrary, my contention is that it is precisely because the effects of macro policy are wide ranging that we wish to consider applying such tools at this time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, a number of the policies that I discussed associated with interest and exchange rates, have the benefit of being fast to implement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Budgetary measures take time to draw up and disburse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, interest and exchange rate policies can be rolled out once the decision has been made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the suggestions I made are complementary in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The monetary measures deployed to cool inflation are contractionary, as they should be, by design.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To limit the risk of derailing a still-fragile economy and recovery, we should offset this effect with fiscal measures that are modestly expansionary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government’s support package is consistent with this, but this risks being unwound by the impending GST hike.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Instead, what we want is a macro policy stance that is broadly neutral, which is what is appropriate for our economy at this stage of the business cycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, we want to downshift and tap on the brakes to contain inflation, but pumping on a wee bit of gas with limited government spending that helps keep the engine from stalling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To some extent, this is inevitable; the nature of macroeconomic policymaking is often technical in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, it is possible to summarise my main suggestions in a few sentences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will respond to the Motion in two parts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will start by addressing the macro picture, before zooming in to the micro picture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: A hallmark of our Government since Independence has been our ability to look long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We see the big picture, the macro picture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This includes assessing the world and the winds of change, as well as identifying the trends, opportunities and challenges for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In this House yesterday, I shared our economic outlook for Singapore, including our GDP growth and inflation projections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For the sake of brevity in this response, I shall not repeat those details and Members can refer to my speech yesterday.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: What I would like to focus on in my response is how we have planned for and laid foundations for the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, we maintain a stable macroeconomic environment so that businesses and households can make economic decisions with confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And a core tenet is our exchange rate-centred monetary policy which has helped us manage inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: During this period of rising inflationary pressures, MAS has pre-emptively tightened monetary policy since October last year, as the Member has observed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This longstanding policy has directly helped dampen imported inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's point on food prices, as well as energy prices, let me dive deeper.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Second, we continue to build our trade links to the world, to diversify our sources of imports and exports, even as the world is experiencing a retreat of globalisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We concluded the world's largest Free Trade Agreement (FTA), the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (RCEP), in November 2020, and are part of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have also signed the Pacific Alliance-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (PASFTA) in January and are on track to conclude an FTA with Mercosur.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have also signed Digital Economy Agreements (DEAs), Digital Economy Partnership Agreements (DEPAs) and are in the process of negotiating a green economy agreement with Australia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These trade agreements help us to diversify our imports, open markets for our businesses and future-proof our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Third, we continue to stay open and connected to the world and to innovation, investments and talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And despite the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, we attracted S$11.8 billion in Fixed Asset Investments (FAI) last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have secured significant investments, for example, Sanofi has committed to setting up a €400 million vaccine production facility in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These inbound investments create good jobs for Singaporeans, make our economy vibrant and competitive and prepare us for the next pandemic – long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Overall, strong growth will support job creation, wage growth and help address inflationary pressures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, as we continue to plan and execute our macro and strategic plans, we also keep our eye firmly on the micro – the ground picture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we plan and execute the macro, but we also keep our eye firmly on what is happening on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is reflected in how we navigated Singapore through the COVID-19 crisis and support Singaporeans and local businesses during this period of rising costs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: During the height of COVID-19, we committed close to S$100 billion over the last two years, part of it to support businesses hit by COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also rolled out initiatives, such as our SingapoRediscovers Vouchers (SRVs) for our embattled tourism sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Collectively, about $300 million in vouchers and out-of-pocket payments were generated through SRV transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This provided crucial support to our local tourism business.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In anticipation of higher prices, we rolled out support for Singaporeans in Budget 2022, including the Jobs and Business Support Package, to help businesses and workers, as well as the Household Support Package to help households with their daily needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And to help Singaporeans cope with rising inflationary pressures, we also brought forward the implementation of some of the measures, including our CDC Vouchers and Small Business Recovery Grant (SBRG).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The measures included in the package also help our local companies transform and cope with rising energy costs by becoming more energy-efficient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It also provides targeted relief for specific groups, such as self-employed persons, who depend on their vehicles for their livelihoods and, hence, are more adversely affected by energy cost increases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Overall, we designed the package to avoid stoking further inflationary pressures and distorting price signals, while being, as the Member suggested, fiscally responsible and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And as Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said yesterday, if the situation worsens significantly, we would be prepared to do more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On MAS' monetary policy response to inflation, more specifically, we need to recognise that the global nature of the price pressures we are facing is affecting all of our trading partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The sharp pick-up of inflation of food and oil prices since Q4 last year, principally, reflects the effects of serious disruptions of global supply due to the Ukraine-Russia conflict.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, it is inevitable, as the Member had mentioned, that some of these prices will affect our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Many Singaporeans do accept that the situation requires some adjustments to the high prices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Given the circumstances, I will explain a few points below.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: How MAS decides on the extent of its tightening of the exchange rate takes many different factors into account.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Foremost is the fact that a strengthening exchange rate cannot fully offset global prices without causing immediate negative consequences on growth and, therefore, the labour market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Indeed, this is precisely the reason why many advanced central banks are guarded in the speed and also the extent to which they will hike interest rates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This monetary policy action, in and of itself, has attendant spillover effects that we must all take into account in a very uncertain, dynamic and also challenging economic environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Therefore, a judicious blend of tight monetary policy and targeted supportive fiscal policy, carefully calibrated, is most appropriate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On indexing financial assistance payments to inflation, I would just like to say that the Government regularly reviews our schemes to take into account needs and affordability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And inflation is one of the many factors taken into consideration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have responded to the Member's Motion by articulating our Government's macro and micro approaches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We plan and execute for the long term and, at the same time, continue to have the dexterity to zoom in into the details that matter on the ground to Singaporeans and Singaporean businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Indeed, the livelihoods of our people are not a theoretical exercise to us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Rather, we focus on strong job creation and wage growth as the best ways to help Singaporeans tide over these immediate difficult times and ensure that we have sufficient resources to tackle the long-term challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The mindset and bias towards action have allowed us to weather storms and seize opportunities throughout our history.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is our commitment to Singapore and we will continue to do our utmost to deliver on this commitment, especially in these challenging times.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I adjourn the House pursuant to the Standing Order.
